evidence.section_title: Insights from Cowichan: A Hybrid Approach to Understanding Suicide in One First Nations' Collective
evidence.quote: Twenty-one interviews were conducted with members of the Cowichan Tribes to understand reasons for suicide in one community.
Semistructured interviews were conducted with 21 tribal members
The 21 interviews were completed in three demographic groups within the community: elders (age 55+), youth (age 10–18), and other enrolled tribal members (18–54).

evidence.section_title: Insights from Cowichan: A Hybrid Approach to Understanding Suicide in One First Nations' Collective
evidence.quote: Its aims are to understand the meanings of suicide for members of the Cowichan Tribes, a Canadian First Nation, and to find explanations for suicidal behavior among tribal members.
understand how Cowichan tribal members make sense of suicide
The Cowichan Tribes represent the largest First Nations band in British Columbia

Mandated and funded by Canada's federal government, and implemented largely by Christian churches, the Indian Act authorized the forced removal of Indian children to residential schools (Haig-Brown, 1988; Miller, 1987; Trevithick, 1998) as vectors of assimilation. In this way, children were removed from the influence of their families, their cultural communities, and their traditional homelands. The repercussions of this policy have been complex and devastating. When asked, "Why are Cowichan people dying by suicide?" a 57-yearold man named Kyle, forcefully implicated residential schools:

The present inquiry is part of a larger ethnographic study designed to understand how Cowichan tribal members make sense of suicide in relation to contemporary and historical experiences.

evidence.section_title: Insights from Cowichan: A Hybrid Approach to Understanding Suicide in One First Nations' Collective
evidence.quote: Qualitative analysis identified explanatory constructs proposed by the interpersonal theory as well as negative conditions stemming from colonialism, as proposed by settler colonial theory. These results argue that Indigenous suicidal behavior is best understood from an interdependent standpoint.

[009_the_interpersonal_theory_of_suicide][page/3/Text/12] Explanations for suicidal behavior at the individual level were provided in relation to three constructs highlighted by the interpersonal theory: acquired capacity to enact lethal self-harm, including violence or exposure to violence and suicidal behavior; thwarted belongingness, including loneliness and absence of reciprocal caring relations; and perceived burdensomeness, including perceived liability and self-hate (Joiner, 2007).; [009_the_interpersonal_theory_of_suicide][page/4/Text/10] All these factors are associated with suicide risk (Van Orden et al., 2010).; [009_the_interpersonal_theory_of_suicide][page/5/Text/5] Importantly, when each participant was asked directly if he or she wished to die by suicide, the answer was no—all shared a desire to live.
